svg.title: Credentials and preferences — okfy security explainer
svg.desc: What the tool writes to the browser, and how it treats what it reads back. Six keys live in local storage and one in session storage; there is no cookie, no indexed database and no cache entry of the tool's own. The local storage keys are the assistant's settings, which hold the provider key and the OAuth token only when remembering is on; a flag recording that the acknowledgement was accepted; the host whose provider notice was dismissed; the player volume, clamped to zero through one; the interface language, checked against the tool's own list; and the assistant panel width, clamped to three hundred and twenty pixels up to ninety per cent of the window. The seventh key, a short-lived OAuth verifier and state, lives in session storage and is removed on sign-out. Everything is a preference except the provider key: a key you type lives in the page's memory by default and is gone when the tab closes, and it is written to storage only when the Remember the key in this browser box is ticked, after which it is unencrypted and readable by any script on the origin. Unticking it and saving leaves it out of the next write, and signing out clears the OAuth token from storage. The write is an allowlist rather than a dump of the settings: a fixed field list, and for each provider the base URL, the auth kind, the API version and the OAuth endpoint, its scopes and the client ID, which are not secrets and are therefore stored either way, with the key and the access token written only when remembering is on. The transcript, the tool results, the graph, the decks and the preview history are never written. The read rebuilds the configuration rather than trusting the blob: the tool's own defaults come first, then only the field names it knows, then only the providers it has, each merged onto its own defaults, and then the language is checked against the tool's list while the width and the volume are clamped; a parse failure or a blob that is not what it claims simply yields the defaults. Every read and every write is guarded, so a browser that blocks storage, such as a private window or a full quota, still works and simply remembers nothing. Nothing about a bundle is stored, so clearing site data or using a private window forgets everything without leaving a trace of what was read. The consequence is that the stored key is only as safe as the origin's own script discipline, which is why the renderer never turns bundle text into markup and the policy forbids inline event handlers; storage is per origin, so a bundle should live on an origin of its own.
svg.text: OKFY · SECURITY EXPLAINER
Credentials and preferences
One opt-in secret and a handful of preferences, in this browser and nowhere else
1 · What is kept, and where
Every key the tool writes, and what it holds
key
holds
okfy.assistant
the assistant's settings; the key and token only when remembered
okfy.assistant.ack
that the acknowledgement was accepted
okfy.assistant.warn
the host whose provider notice was dismissed
okfy.volume
the player volume, clamped to 0 … 1 on the way in
okfy.lang
the interface language, checked against the tool's own list
okfy.as.width
the assistant panel width, clamped to 320 px … 90 % of the window
okfy.as.pkce
a short-lived OAuth verifier, in sessionStorage, removed on sign-out
Six keys in localStorage and one in sessionStorage: no cookie, no IndexedDB and no cache entry of the tool's own.
2 · The one secret
The provider key, and the OAuth access token
in memory by default
a key you type lives in the page's memory and is gone when the tab closes
opt in to remember
one checkbox: Remember the key in this browser
then it is unencrypted
written under okfy.assistant, readable by any script on the origin
untick and save
the next write leaves it out, so the stored copy goes away
the OAuth token
the same rule, and cleared from storage on sign-out
Its safety therefore rests on the page never running bundle text: the escaping rules in input handling are what
keep that set of scripts at one — the page's own — and the policy forbids inline event handlers.
3 · What is written
The write is an allowlist, not a dump of the settings
the fields
a fixed list: model, provider, stream, temperature, tokens, budget, speak, device
the provider
base URL, auth kind, API version, and the OAuth endpoint, scopes and client ID
not secrets
so those are stored whether or not a key is remembered
the key, the token
written only when remembering is on
Never written: the transcript, the tool results, the graph, the decks, the preview history.
Storage holds settings, never what was read: a bundle's content, its page text and its links are not copied into it.
4 · What is read back
The read rebuilds the settings rather than trusting the blob
start from defaults
the tool's own defaults are the base, not the stored object
copy a known list
only the field names it knows are copied from the parsed JSON
keep known providers
a provider the tool does not have is dropped; each survivor is merged onto its defaults
validate the rest
the language is checked against the tool's list; the width and volume are clamped
and if it is junk
a parse failure, or a blob that is not what it claims, yields the defaults
Every read and every write is guarded, so a browser that blocks storage — a private window, a full quota — still
works: it simply remembers nothing.
5 · What is never stored
Nothing about a bundle, or about a session, is written
no bundle content
no page text, no frontmatter, no links
no transcript
the chat and the tool results live in memory for the session
no graph state
expansion pages, the focus and the preview history are per session
no deck
a deck you build is gone on reload unless the bundle declares it
so clearing site data
or a private window, forgets everything and leaves no trace of what was read
One key is the whole of it: it is opt-in, it is readable by any script on the origin, and what protects it is that
no bundle text ever becomes script. Storage is per origin, so keep a bundle on an origin of its own.
